demos.title: Accessible DOM Card Battler
demos.summary: Turn-based card combat is discrete UI, not a render loop. Semantic buttons, focus, and live regions are the game surface.
demos.why: A turn-based card game is a sequence of explicit player decisions. DOM controls already provide keyboard operation, focus, and announcements, so Canvas or a continuous loop would add complexity without serving the rules.

demos.title: High-DPI Canvas Arcade Dodger
demos.architecture: Canvas 2D / variable delta / DPR backing store
demos.summary: Real-time dodging needs a pixel surface and frame-delta movement, plus blur/visibility handling so held keys and stalls stay honest.
demos.why: Hazards move continuously and collision is spatial. Canvas 2D is the simplest pixel surface. Variable delta is enough for arcade feel if pathological frames are clamped; a fixed step is not required yet.

demos.title: Fixed-Step Platformer
demos.summary: Jumping onto platforms is sensitive to frame-rate variation, so simulation steps stay fixed while rendering interpolates.
demos.why: Platform collision and jump arcs change if the physics step follows the display refresh. A bounded fixed step keeps gameplay stable; interpolation is presentation only and is not claimed as cross-platform determinism.

demos.title: Manifest-Driven Generated-Art Adventure
demos.summary: Runtime never invents filenames or atlas frames. Spec, local generation, hashes, and the manifest are the only asset authority.
demos.why: The lesson is the verified asset lifecycle, not a paid image API. Procedural local art is enough if every runtime lookup goes through logical IDs in an emitted, validated manifest.

demos.title: WebGL2 Particle Arena
demos.summary: A particle count large enough to justify GPU instancing, with compile errors, context loss, and quality controls made visible.
demos.why: Thousands of independently moving particles are a GPU problem. Canvas 2D fill would hide the architecture being demonstrated. WebGL2 instancing is used because the visual load requires it, not as a default engine.

demos.title: Accessible Puzzle Museum
demos.architecture: DOM / semantic exhibits / no game loop
demos.summary: Three puzzle rooms prove a browser game can be documents, forms, and focus — not a canvas by default.
demos.why: These puzzles are discrete logic problems with instructions and results. Semantic HTML already models rooms, controls, and status. A canvas loop would fight keyboard and screen-reader use.

demos.title: Two-Bone IK Creature Sandbox
demos.summary: A creature limb follows a pointer with an analytical two-bone solver, reach clamps, and fixtures for extreme targets.
demos.why: Limb presentation is geometry, not a physics engine. An analytical two-bone solver is the smallest correct tool; iterative CCD would be unjustified for a two-segment arm.

demos.title: Swarm Collision Broadphase Lab
demos.summary: A measurement bench, not a game level: same swarm, two algorithms, clustered pathology included.
demos.why: Spatial hashing is an optimization that can lose on clustered data. The architecture is the comparison itself — naive pairs stay available so claims are measured rather than assumed.

demos.title: Offline Strategy Simulation
demos.summary: A small map whose End Turn work is heavy enough to leave the UI, with versioned saves and explicit corruption handling.
demos.why: The UI is a turn sheet; the expensive part is deterministic world resolution. A worker is justified for that calculation. IndexedDB is justified because saves are structured, versioned documents — not a few settings keys.

demos.title: Shared-Memory Field Simulator
demos.summary: A field large enough to show data-path cost, with SHARED MEMORY vs FALLBACK TRANSFER/COPY labeled in the UI.
demos.why: SharedArrayBuffer is a security-gated concurrency tool, not a default. This demo exists to detect isolation, use SAB only when legal, and keep a copy/transfer path so the lesson still works without it.
